newsitem.title: USA: Amelio's turnaround medicine was no cure for Apple.
newsitem.headline: Amelio's turnaround medicine was no cure for Apple.

text.p: Gilbert Amelio was hailed as a turnaround specialist who could nurse Apple Computer Inc. back to health.

But 17 months after he took charge of the Cupertino, Calif.-based company, the turnaround specialist is out of a job, becoming the latest in a long list of top industry executives who have failed to turn Apple around.
"I said when Gil Amelio took over, it was a tough job," Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak said in an interview after Apple announced Amelio's departure in a tersely worded statement.

Analysts and computer industry experts said Amelio's formal management style clashed with Apple's culture of youthful exuberance. He once said wearing a tie around Apple's headquarters campus helped set him apart.
But some said he never dug deeply enough to understand Apple's problems.
Fred Anderson, a highly-regarded financial executive who Amelio brought in to be chief financial officer, told reporters Wednesday the board was unhappy with Apple's performance under Amelio.
Experts who knew Amelio were not surprised by his departure.

"When he first went there I predicted that it wouldn't work," said Dan Hutcheson, the president of VLSI Research Inc. who had worked with Amelio as a computer chip industry consultant before Amelio joined Apple.

Hutcheson noted that co-founder Steve Jobs, former Pepsi executive John Scully and Michael Spindler had each failed at Apple's helm, and said, "I think that Apple was a doomed company where there was not something anybody could do with it."

Wozniak said he had not been actively involved in Apple's management during Amelio's tenure. But he said he had agreed it had needed to cut back in its reorganization and was hopeful that it would recover.
"I just hope we get somebody that's really good at judging customers and where they are now and in the future," he said.
"I am hopeful that it can come back. I know that there are a lot of people that want that."

Amelio, 54, literally wrote the book on corporate turnarounds, co-authoring "Profit from Experience: The National Semiconductor Story of Tranformation Management" which was published within days of his taking Apple's helm.
Amelio, who led corporate turnarounds at both National Semiconductor and Rockwell Communications Systems before that, gave himself 100 days to come up with a plan that would set Apple back on course.

After carefully scrutinizing Apple's position and getting his own management team in place, Amelio said he was confident he knew what the computer maker's problems were and declared triumphantly last spring that "they are fixable."

But Apple continued to stumble. Its worldwide share of the personal computer market dwindled to as low as 5.3 percent last year as the company laid off thousands of workers, lost talented senior management and posted net losses of $1.6 billion over the six quarters.
The company's stock has been trading at the lowest level in 12 years in recent sessions, closing down 6 cents at $13.69 on Nasdaq Wednesday, and even vague takeover rumors have subsided.

"What surprised me is that he sort of treated Apple like a conventional turnaround where the company is mismanaged, not mistructured," Hutcheson said, adding that Apple had failed to maintain a 5-to-10 year technological lead over the PC industry.

"Apple's problem wasn't management, but that it was caught between the 50s and the 90s and you couldn't change that," he added. "They'd allowed themselves in the heyday to develop a culture that was pretty loose and free and the idea was that if you worship the technology the money would come."
